review:
I started with Rome: Total War and it was a great game. You picked an empire to control and used diplomacy, force, and cunning to grow. You manage armies, cities, and special units (spys/diplomats) in order to conquor Europe and surrounding areas.

What Medieval II: Total War did was took Rome: Total War and made it even better. With the same mechanics and the addition of converting cities to forts and vice-versa the gameplay becomes even better. New units, new Factions, and a new map gave this series a well deserved title.

I myself consider Medieval II: Total War to be the best game in the entire Total War franchise because instead of dumbing down the game (which is becoming rampant in the game industry) they took what they had and improved upon it instead.

I recommend you buy this game if you are an intelligent person who enjoys to plan things out and act upon them with patience and coordination.

Thanks for reading.

In case you haven't played any Total War games, this game isn't the best graphically (it's over 15 years old at this point, 2021), but it can offer you hundreds (maybe even thousands) of hours in playtime. You get to play either the Grand campaign or historical battles or custom battles. The grand campaign is the most fun, since after choosing a faction you get to manage cities and command big armies through the Old World in the medieval ages (if you play for enough turns you get gunpowder for gunners and cannons). For battles you can either auto-resolve them (not recommending it unless you are short on time) or fight them in real time, where you (in a way) get to a custom battle based on where you are. In those fights you command units that are comprised of dozens or even a hundred men and there is decent versatility since all factions have swordsmen, pikemen, archers and cavalry without feeling the same. As for the historical battles, they are fights with preset armies for both you and your enemies and they are rather hard in my opinion.

To those that have played other Total War games, I think this is the best of the bunch and I have played Rome, Rome 2, Shogun 2, Medieval 1 (don't try it. Trust me on this. It's rather painful to play now), the Warhammer ones and even Troy. While all total games have their charm (Except Troy. F that game. If you want I can tell my opinion on that in the comments), I think that the more recent ones focus way too much on battles, an aspect that was always pretty good and needed little to no improvement (Except the AI, but they don't seem to care about this) and they gloss over city and economy management (yes, they are still there, but barely). In this one, you have the most options: First of all, you get to choose between the more defendable and more military-oriented castle or the more economy-oriented city (and you actually need both, or you can easily go bankrupt). And secondly, you get lots of buildings that improve a lot of aspects in the city, like ports, farms,churches etc. If it had the city-viewing option from Rome it would be perfect.


TL;DR: This is in my opinion the best Total War game you can find, especially if like me, you love knights. 9.5/10 (I will break my own rule of not putting a grade beyond 9/10. The only other game I am considering doing this for when I get to it is Skyrim)

For a while, I didn't understand how people could think that Medieval 2 was the best Total War game. It seemed too dated and clunky for me to ever enjoy. After giving it a fair chance and finishing a campaign I realize now how wrong I was. Medieval 2 has become my favorite Total War game, but even if i'm trying to be unbiased, it is still the highest quality Total War game I have ever played. I know now how many steps back Creative Assembly have taken, and how much depth the newer games lack compared to this one. 

Coming from the newer Total War games, I never would have guessed that Medieval 2 has a really fun roleplaying element. The "traits" system works differently in this game, and it lets you add personality and complexity to generals, turning them into shining pillars of chivalry, or deplorable, malevolent warmongers, through your actions in war. These extreme poles of morality come with their own effects and bonuses. Dread leads to decreased enemy morale in battle, where as chivalry leads to increased friendly morale in battle as well as extra population growth in settlements. When generals inevitably die, in combat or of old age, it can be emotional, because you were there with them from the start, built them up from nothing, and watched them conquer, only to have to watch them die. This kind of connection to these characters gives such a layer of intricacy to this game that the newer games don't really have, especially Warhammer, as in that game faction leaders and lords are immortal gods of slaughter. 

In Medieval 2, men win wars, not magic tricks. The morale system is amazing, you're rewarded for out maneuvering the enemy. Breaking their morale is one of the most satisfying things in gaming. This game is a cavalry lovers wet dream, this is easily the best tw game for cav, heavy cav hits like a truck, while horse archers are effective at dancing around enemies while whittling them down with arrows. After playing this game, cav in other tw games feels like a wet noodle (except Attila). There is much more room for strategy, no dropping down magic spells on giant blobs of enemies. Taking heavy losses takes a toll on the player, units don't magically replenish themselves, and the weight of death can be felt, because you are a human, fighting and killing other humans. At the end of the day, in my opinion, human conflict will always be more interesting and meaningful than the conflict between fantastical races and magical creatures. There are also little things about the battles that the newer games lack entirely. Dynamic weather and time are two things in this game that blew my mind playing for the first time. Battles drag on in the game world, seemingly for hours, (just like real pitched battles in history) and this is reflected by the in game weather and time. Rainfall, sandstorms, fog, are all things that can come and go during the battle. You will often fight battles that start in the afternoon and end at sunset, or begin in darkness and end with the sunrise. Seeing this mechanic in a game this old after coming from the newer tw games really makes me wonder why they scrapped this feature.

On the campaign side of things, you have diplomacy, which is somewhat complex for a game this old, but still not nearly as complex as Paradox games. You control your own diplomats, in order to initiate diplomacy with another faction, you literally have to move one of your diplomats to one of their cities, as opposed to a few clicks of your mouse in the newer games. Merchants are a way for you to earn a bit of cash on the side, by finding valuable resources to bring back to your capital. Spies are helpful when it comes to waging a successful war, or finding out information about rivals. Assassinations can be attempted on many characters (including the pope) and this adds to the sense of mortality of characters in this game. All of this adds to immersion quite a bit. As the campaign progresses, time moves on, armor and weapons become more advanced, one must adapt and modernize their armies and strategies in order to keep up with the rest of the world. 

Rewrite history, turn heroes into villains, turn despots into saints, conquer the known world as fast as you can, or try and follow history as accurately as you can, it's really up to you. It might seem like I am taking shots at the Total War: Warhammer games, but I still think those games are good, just not nearly as good as this one. I also highly recommend the stainless steel mod for the best experience possible.

Objectively, the best Total War entry. It improves on Rome: Total War in almost every single way. It has a few quirks that are vastly overshadowed by its perfections.

The age it wears, it wears well because when this game released, the gaming industry landscape was vastly different and much healthier. Developers were still geeks and nerds that wanted to play the games they created, not bloated HR money laundering schemes. Creative Assembly is manned by a completely different crew.

[i] You can see and feel the passion the developers had for Medieval II. [/i]

The charming UI, to the immersive music, to the campaign design, to even small details like armor upgrades being visible on units. The unit/faction balancing is nigh flawless with each faction having their own specialty that makes them unique, and with their campaign position to boot. Every single system in this game hums in harmony with the others, and its clear the development team had a CLEAR vision for this game. This isn't so much a one-for-one historical game, but its basis is believable and immersive enough you care for your characters and country. Units feel weighty, and tactics are rewarded over raw unit stats.

The game rewards player ingenuity and doesn't spoon feed you like a child. AI battle difficulty hits the sweet spot because the difficulty specifically targets towards players SKILL level with unit tactics rather than RAW unit statistics. 

[i] Almost all further entries in the series miss this point. [/i]

A few flaws I can think of are the notoriously terrible pathfinding during siege battles and wonky camera controls, with some bugs, however none I've encountered that are campaign ending.

This game is SO perfect, you can start to identify the cut content the developers wanted to implement more of, but sadly never made it.

Modders have transformed this masterpiece into the quintessential generational strategy and unit tactics video game. Its 20th birthday is coming up, and this means inevitably that the men and women that enjoyed this game can do so with their children. 

If any former Total War dev or current one reads this.... Medieval II is the standard and I'm not talking just about features, I'm talking things making sense and harmony of the various systems that create memorable scenarios and situations that are player created. 

Example: If you have a plague ridden city and you put a character in it, chances are they'll get sick. If you then place said character in another city, that city becomes plagued. The game rewards you for your ingenuity. You can use this feature to create emergent gameplay and NUKE enemy factions' populations/characters/armies(or your own). There are so many hidden features that are unspoken because YOU play the game, not the game playing YOU. 

If you try any of the newer titles and you can see the difference like night and day... Nobody is going to play Pharaoh or Troy in 20 years, let alone with their child.

You generally don't play this game in vanilla, but; if you do you'll find that its simply a joyride of yesteryears gaming. Enjoy these kinds of games, because we'll likely never see anything as passionate as them again.

This is, without a doubt, the best the series ever got. Oh, what's that? You don't care about the Medieval period? My Brother in Christ, there are mods for every conceivable setting you can imagine from Tolkien to the Thirty Years War; from Elder Scrolls to the same era as Empire - all on the absolute best engine the series has ever had for actual tactical gameplay. That's right, ain't no cheesing mechanics with OP hero units in these parts. Sure there's exploits - all old games like this have had their meta surgically dissected at this point. But unlike later games, this wasn't built intentionally with exploits. In fact, most of the meta you have to learn on your own. Ironically this is because the tutorial campaign wasn't finished, but what this does produce is a constantly rewarding experience of learning what Statecraft is within the game on the fly. This gives you almost infinite replayability as upon learning a new mechanic or strategy you'll want to apply it on your next Grand Campaign.

Oh, I'm sorry: you think TW Campaign Maps are shallow compared to Paradox games? Well if you like spreadsheets, yeah you're not gonna enjoy this game. But once again: I present to you the innumerable submods designed to bring things you're familiar with from games like Crusader Kings into this game's campaign. Be warned: some of these are indeed hit or miss, but overall the campaign gives otherwise inevitably dry curated skirmish battles meaning and punch. There's actually a decent amount here for those of us who enjoy roleplaying in our Grand Strategy games as an epic saga is crafted before your very eyes. Very rarely will two campaigns play out the same way.

My strong advice to all new players is to start with Vanilla. Once you've exhausted that, start looking into mods. All the expansions are worth playing for shorter more thematic campaigns that will put your skills to the test with new mechanics, unit types and unique maps. But if you think you grasp TW enough, feel free to jump straight to mods. Hot-take: the Warhammer mod is a better TW adaptation of the franchise than the retail release will ever be and this simple fact is why CA & Sega occasionally sneak patches that seem to, mechanically, hurt this mod the most.

No matter what becomes of the franchise, this entry represents the peak. This is where they got what Total War is supposed to be right. This was the best the gameplay ever was for people who care about real strategy, tactical warfare and not gimmicks and memes. There's plenty of those here, but unlike with new versions it's not the only thing the game is good for.

Multiplayer is best with friends and all the mods work with it. Brave public lobbies at your own risk. There's no way beyond Gentleman's Honor to set rules for army comps to prevent people - especially in Vanilla - from getting a stack of six Venetian General's Bodyguard. But with friends you'll be needing a towel on standby to wipe the sweat off your face with how intense it gets with a group of people who know their stuff. Your Discord will become absolutely silent as you and the homies focus up. 

Like I said: this is what Total War should've been. If you want to understand why people have such strong feelings about it and the original Rome is too dated for you, check this out. If you're that stuck on Antiquity - I understand - Europa Barbororum II is the mod for you. It's the same time period as that game with mind-blowing added realism, historical accuracy and an expanded campaign map.

I'd say it's worth the full retail price. But I do have my gumption about paying, today, what I paid for a game twenty years ago. Either way, pick it up and thank me later.

Medieval 2 might be the greatest strategy game ever created. 

This isn't nostalgia speaking. I didn't touch the game until 2015. It's that good. By some miracle, this buggy 2005 sequel with barely functioning AI manages to have grand campaigns and battles with a myriad of depth and replayability. On top of that, there's over a decades worth of mods; some extremely well crafted. It's kind of amazing how the sequel to Rome: Total War (widely considered to be one of the best games of all time) manages to improve on nearly every aspect of Rome while playing differently. 

The campaigns genuinely feel like you're constructing an empire. Rather than a boring "build this to recruit this," there's a broad amount of customization and micromanaging that leeways into specialized areas. Some cities will be used as a trade hub. Some castles will be used to raise knights. Some castles will be used to create professional infantry and level up armour. Ect... If you're engaged with the building system, you end up with hub areas that will affect what units and strategies you'll use on certain fronts. In addition, cities (and the campaign in general) have many systems that are abusable by the player. Don't want to besiege a settlement? Send in spies to create unrest. Don't want the AI repairing damages to its cities? Blockade its port. Don't like the pope pestering you? Start a crusade to take back Jerusalem. Speaking of the Pope, many of the overarching hierarchies in the campaign are what make it so special to this day. One of the problems with Rome 1 was, after the player took the city of Rome, there were no more special elements in place to prevent the player from steamrolling everyone. While the Civil War with 3 other Roman factions was interesting, it pretty much marked the end of any challenge. Medieval 2 has the church you constantly need to deal with in some manner, the other religious which will ally against you if you pose a threat to their existence, the invasion of the Mongols at a dedicated point in time, and constant advancements in technology that change the game. It's kind of overwhelming for a first time play through, but I wouldn't have it any other way. It's great. If you act with the grace of the Roman Empire the whole world will be united under multiple bands knocking on your front door.

In a game where nearly all factions have access to heavy infantry and cavalry, it's marvelous how there is still faction diversity. While not as pronounced as Rome 1's, it's there. Different kingdoms have a general set of identical units, and then access to more special units, and then they're own unique units. This is just enough to make every faction play differently (mostly. There are a couple of redundancies). More importantly is how the battles play, and Medieval 2 has, by a country mile, thee most elements and options of every Total War game to this date. There's archers, crossbowmen, skirmishers, spearmen, heavy infantry, 2-handed units, pikemen/halberdiers, firearms,  cannons, ancient siege equipment, light cavalry, heavy cavalry, and horse archers. Each unit has its own role, and (unlike later Total Wars) they don't exist in a basic rock-paper-scissors format. Rather, a lot of it boils down to the tactics each player employs. It's kind of hard to explain without giving an example, so I'll go over how the knight works. 

Knights are heavily armored, have a powerful charge, can break any unit of infantry in one rear charge, and are highly mobile. The downside is they're expensive, suck when they don't have room to maneuver, and are expensive, meaning they don't trade cost efficiently on a 1 to 1 basis. You would think this means Knights just charge everything, but that really isn't the case. Multiple units have situationally dependent counters. All ranged units will get destroyed by knights, but can trade favorably if they can get enough volleys off in time. Spearmen and Heavy Infantry counter knights well because they get a bonus against cav and have the same melee stats but contain more men per unit, respectively. So infantry can defeat knights, but not if the knights charge from behind. But getting behind an enemy requires some outmaneuvering, which will require other units. Light Cav will straight-up lose to Knights in an honest engagement, but can harass Knights with a charge whenever their back is undefended, while also being able to outrun Knights. Horse archers pretty heavily counter knights, but not if they get cornered. Pikemen chew through cavalry, but are outright useless when hit on a flank.

Do you see why this is so amazing? Knights are about breaking the enemy by plowing right into a unit (preferably from behind). However, they can still charge head on and win, but the trade may not be economical. With that said, it still may create a breakthrough for the rest of the army to capitalize on. Knights are countered by Horse Archers, but that situation can be completely turned around if the Horse Archers are outmaneuvered by the Knights. Instead of "I have X unit therefore I counter Y," Medieval 2 is about "I have X unit in Z situation therefore I can do A, B, and C against Y each with their own pros and cons."

I feel like the multiplayer being active to this day speaks to the quality of the battles. They are a complex mind game about exploiting thee most minor of advantages to completely topple an entire army. Medieval 2 has its flaws (such as the AI being well below mediocre. The micromanaging of settlements in the late game is abhorrently tedious), and it fails at properly communicating a lot of its core mechanics, but it's an absolutely beautiful game.

Medieval II Total War is considered by many to be the Magnum Opus of Creative Arts total war series. With Medieval II allowing you to play as a plethora of nations across the old world, each with their own rosters that emphasize how these people managed to conquer and maintain their independence in an era of increased centralization.

The biggest change from its predecessor was the inclusion of a crusades and Jihads. As the game takes place during the Crusades, this is a welcome addition which also forces the AI to fight the player or other AI for territories it would not traditionally go after under the guise of reclaiming territory in the name of the faith.

The additional challenge is an important one as it prevents Eastern Players from expanding to aggressively due to the new imminent threats. The final main strength of the game is in its transitions of warfare. Within the first 100 tubes, the introduction of gunpowder to armies marks a major shift in European Warfare. With the game brilliantly shifting focus of warfare from short meleé’s to a ranged game with emphasis on closing speed he distance. This is then altered a final time with the introduction of the cannon, primarily as field artillery. This shift of warfare occurring twice in the game forces the player and AI to rapidly adapt to the shift or be left behind and with the invasions from the East, test the ability if any player in the face of the horde.

Medieval 2 Total War is the definition of a turn based strategy game, executed in a phenomenal way, with the game bringing players back to it time and time again over its dynamic mechanics and stellar replay. One of the major selling points for Medieval II, for me personally, is that the pace is far slower than Shogun II, Rome II or Warhammer I. It is not that the game is *slow* but rather one does not feel constantly rushed to power play, or lose. It can also be a very difficult game. One slip up diplomatically, such as a careless excommunication can lead to other kingdoms dog-piling on you. 
Meaning, simplified, the game models the Catholic church as follows: kingdoms vote for a pope, who will come from one of the Catholic countries. The Pope will have favorites, and might pose e.g. ceasefires on warring Catholic factions, with either loss of favor or excommunication as a reward if the ceasefire is broken: excommunicated kingdoms face unrest and possibly Crusades by former Catholic friends. Pretty cool idea, even if the execution is a bit half-baked. 
One major thing for me is also the fact, that ranged units feel *heavy*-- it is not only the number of casualties which longbows or Italian crossbows can cause, but the feel for the weapons. What I disliked about Warhammer was, that archers in that game feel to be shooting pieces of straw. The feedback from hitting the enemy ranks is not there in Warhemmer TW. In Medieval II the sound effects for chain mail being pierced, and the fast moving arrows coming down as a cloud of death are on point. Fire rate is slow, and it makes perfect sense to keep auto fire off, as not to risk friendly fire and e.g. break a cavalry charge with a well timed volley. 
Melee tends to be messy, slow and exhausting, especially for modded, and higher difficulties. Generally, clean victories only come to the side who outmanoeuvres the enemy and gets to charge home to a flank with cavalry, or manages to split the hostile army and deal with the pockets one by one. 

Mods are Great for Medieval II. Highlights are probably Third Age: TW for the LotR theme, and the historical Stainless Steel. I like the very basic Darthmod, as there really is no need for total conversion-- vanilla has all the bits and pieces needed for a classic, just maybe in need for the community to fine tune somewhat. 

The game shows its age in sieges, where it is very difficult to get units off the walls (or on), and the same problem rears at times in field battles, as the unit AI needs some prodding to reform the line after combat. Cavalry sometimes abruptly slows its charge, or halts it entirely. 
Reinforcement mechanics can be irritating, as one needs to replenish units in a city, or a castle, which houses the appropriate production building. Very annoying, if taking an enemy city, and the AI has done very little military building. 

But the good by far outweighs the bad. Probably my preferred TW game, even if dated. Recommended!

I switched to Scotland ._.

Medieval II is like a lobotomized alcoholic son. It regularly has 30iq moments and is terribly gangly and unruly to handle, but dammit you love it anyway. Yes the soldier models look like wax figures caught in a housefire. Yes they only do what you tell them to 40% of the time. It's a game that is cheeseable to the nth degree, clearly dated, and had problems even in its heyday. Yet, there is an undeniable greatness to Medieval II that makes it a community favorite even after all these years. The thriving mod scene, the content creators, the memes. Underneath all of the eccentricities is one of the better RTS games of its time, and one that has absolutely endless replay value to it. The four bonus campaigns each focus on different aspects of what makes Medieval II good, and I would say three of them are better than the grand campaign. The balance is hysterically busted, yet it can allow for creative solutions to a problem. Everything does have a place. The soundtrack is burned into my skull. Watching little dudes fly through the air when a cannon blast hits them is funny. Listen, this ain't a magnum opus, but it is base and vulgar and frustrating and hilarious and can exercise your think muscle a little. Give it a shot, just have proper expectations of what you are getting in to.

Been playing TWM2 for.. don't remember how many years.. and every time it seems my interest on it start to decay, somehow it renews stronger than ever.
Steam didn't exist when I started playing this game, so after Steam took control of it, I got away from it for a while, but few years ago I decided to come to terms with Steam, and installed a fresh copy of this version.
Then, started to re-try all my old mods, under Steam this time. 
Couple of versions of SS, 6.0 and 6.4 were easy to install and worked right (more about this later).
The same with this other mod, perhaps not so well known: Clouds Across Europe (CAE): found a modernized version, prepared to install under Steam. Equally easy to install and working fine from the scratch.
Now a few words abouth them mods.
SS might be the most likable and lovable TWM mod ever, but for my experience, either under Steam or in the previous stand alone life, it is constantly plagued by sudden CTD interruptions, as early in the game as the 10th Turn. With patience, and using a couple workarounds, I have managed to reach as far as the 653rd Turn, playing with Genoa faction under 6.0 or 455th Turn with the same faction under 6.4.
Mentioned afore workarounds, nothing sophisticated, I can cite these two:
1) Restarting my PC frequently, to clear memory
2) Renouncing to fight battles when large armies are involved, giving away to the AI the decision of the outcome. 
Of course, remedy 1) causes a lot of interruptions in your game session, taking away some fun while benefitting you by giving you time for a short walk, stretch your legs or whatever else.
Remedy 2) is definitely a "fun taker", and an additional obstacle in your quest. At least in my case, I'm used to win most of battles where I take tactical control, even when the odds are against me, whereas you mostly need the odds in your favor for the AI to give you the victory, which forces you to an extra effort in recruiting troops and assembling armies.
With CAE, I have played the Teutonic Order for 180 Turns now, and none single issue has happened yet, the game can be on for hours, even for leaving home at morning and resuming at evening, and the game works without a gltch after the long pause. I can fight the battles as I wish, without worrying about a sudden CTD.
Since CAE so far provides me with what I look for, beyond the TWM2-DE, I haven't tried any other mod yet. I can remember Europe Barbarorum II and Europe On Flames, from the ones I used to play in the stand alone era.
Now, a few tips for the game in general.
1) When defending your sieged settlements (cities, castles, etc.) don't bother to man the walls and try to fend off the assailants. Every settlement has a central square, it's the place where your flags fly. For citties, it is usually a closed space accessible only from four streets, sometimes even less. Place one-two shildrom capable spear units blocking each of those access points to your square. If, in the Deployment stage, you can see where the enemy army is stationed, you place two spear units in the points on the enemy attack direction, an one unit on the other two less threatened points. For artillery, one or two Catapults will do it, if you can afford them. Ballistas won't be enough (unless the attacking army is kind of weak), and Trebuchets/Bombards/Cannon won't be as effective as Catapults, because they are not good to fire parabolic shots over your spear units. Trebuchets can, but they take a long time to recharge and are not as accurate as Catapults in the short/mid range. Four/five archer (or better crossbow) units would round the defending garrison. 
For every important settlement in your realm, that's the size of the garrison you should aspire as a minimun: six schildrom spear units, four crossbow units and one Catapult.
Castles/fortresses are a bit more complicated because the plan doesn't include the central square with few accesses easy to control. They resemble the Keep or central tower design, for smaller settlements with only one ring of walls, the central square will be a place in front of the main building, easily accesible from everywhere and complicated to defend. Larger settlements, with two or more wall rings, will be easier. The central square will be always within the inner ring, and the defensive effort can focus in the one (or two at max) gate that gives access to the square. Place your Catapult on front of the gate (yes, outside the inner wall but close to the gate), and surround it with three or four spear units, and place your missile troops in the walls adjacent to the gate, while keeping two/three spear units in reserve. In this scenario, you can add one or two Trebuchet pieces, well capabla of shooting over the walls. Remember, all the mentions above to the "walls" are referring only to the INNER walls. Here, same as with cities, don't mind the exterior walls.
2) The defensive principle above can be applied to almost all your territory, if you study the map and fortity the bridges that give access to your land, by placing a full army on top of the bridge, you'll be effectively keeping away enemy armies from your cities and settlements. For these armies, plan about nine spear schildrom units (enough for three rings of defense from the bridge head in you side), four/five artillery units of all kind (again, Ballistas not useful here), and five/six missile units (long range archers/crossbowmen the better). Last, one or two Cavalry units to chase and kill routing enemy units. If you manage to establsih a solid frame of fortified bridges, along a with a dense network of forts, garrisoned with replenish units for the frontline (bridges garrisons), your territory will be practically inexpugnable. 
3) Short tip: don't ignore the Mercenary hiring options all your generals have access to. While they are way more expensive than recruiting/training your own troops, it is also true that, punctually and in specific occasions, they can save the day for you, either by reinforcing a defensive force in imminent risk of being attacked, or by reinforcing an attacking army and providing it with decisive superiority for the imminent battle. You can always fire the hired units, once the specific need for the hiring is gone. One feature I have noticed with the mods mentioned above, is the capability of some of your cities to replenish some mercenary units, such as those composed of crowwbowmen. I don't remember this option being available in the original game, but I might be wrong.
4) Final tip: to accomplish the military objectives implicit above (1, 2 and 3), main obstacle usually is lack of money (of course, provided the enemy factions leave you alone for time enough to work on your defenses). To remedy the accute lack of money, there is the ancient option of looting every place, not yours but reachable to your forces. Better yet if you have access to seaports, you can use them as base for "marauding" seaborne armies. Provide these armies with a siege artillery unit (Catapult or better), and send them to attack the rich/poorly defended shores of whatever other nation you can reach to. Of course, be careful of not provoking war with the other strongest factions. Once you capture the settlement, preferably by assault rather than by siege (which wil give time to them to mobilize relief forces), pick the option that gives you more money (usually 2nd or 3rd), and once you occupied the settlement, proceed to dismantle every possible buiding in town, by right clicking it and clicking on the "Recoup" button (the one with the hammer). If you are playing a Christian faction, and the conquered town is also Christian, be aware of sparing the local church from the hammer, unless you want to earn the Pope Excommunication.

Definately has to be one of the best strategy games I have ever played. 
First of all, the gameplay offers a massive choice of nations and units each with their own traits. 17 different factions on top of long and short campaigns give a lot of room for different story paths and immense replayability. The mix of battles, diplomacy, family traits and strategy AI create a truly realistic and immersive game that offers an infinate number of choices to your next move, although the turn-based elements often feel oversimplified. It does have a solid real time combat foundation, but the AI is either really good or really bad depending on the difficulty setting. There is no middle ground. If you are new to real time strategy games, this one has a pretty steep learning curve. Even seasoned players may feel overwhelmed.
One campaign can take days, even months of play time. However, sometimes the game can become a bit taxing to less motivated players (not that I'm complaining) and the AI during battles can often glitch. Whilst these glitches are mostly minor, they nevertheless break your immerson in the game and can be quite annoying when your soldiers glitch about instead of doing as they're told. Despite all its weaknesses, Med 2 is still a briliantly crafted game, its strategy mixed in with impressive graphics and cinematic music will keep you wound up in the Medieval age for thousands of hours.

It's one of CA's best (Total War) games. It beats Empire, it beats Napoleon (which was rather a pile of garbage so that wasn't hard) and it beats Shogun2. I still like Medieval 2 better than anything that came after it.

Still the best Total War game.
